FinanceTab.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

FinanceTab.title: Manchester United: Cost of hiring and firing managers nears £100m
FinanceTab.text:
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.

United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.

The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.

The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.

Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.

Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.

The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".

The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
FinanceTab.text:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

FinanceTab.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
FinanceTab.text:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

SportsTab.title: Lauren Price beats Kotaskova to become undisputed world welterweight champion
SportsTab.text:
Lauren Price dominated Michaela Kotaskova to seal her place in history by becoming undisputed world welterweight champion.

Price, 32, took an unanimous, shut-out decision and the acclaim of the crowd to add the WBO title to her collection and become the first Welsh fighter to claim the accolade of holding all four major world titles.

Already an Olympic champion and world champion from her amateur days, it further underlined her claim as being among the very best in boxing.

But the way in which she did it, extending a perfect professional record to 11 wins from her 11 fights, suggested there could yet be more to come.

Price won every round from every judge in front of a partisan Cardiff crowd, producing an unrelenting pace that punished her opponent at every opportunity.

Although Price could not force a stoppage, there was never any doubt she had done enough against an opponent full of stamina and stubbornness.

Kotaskova, beaten only once, but never stopped in her career, showed real heart but had no answer to Price's expertise.

The Tokyo gold medal winner could celebrate even before the final bell sounded, climbing the corner ropes and into the record books.

It was lapped up by a sell-out Utilita Arena crowd who excitedly acknowledged the achievement and the moment.

Wales has produced 14 world champions, some of them genuine greats.

They include, of course, Joe Calzaghe who so often graced this venue with successful defence after successful defence of his super-middleweight crown.

He never reached undisputed status, though he was able to cross the capital city to go from arena to stadium champion.

That is the next challenge for Price, claiming before she left the ring that more is to come while talk immediately turned to five-weight world champion Claressa Shields as a stadium fight next summer.

That is for the future, but this was a night for history - with the calibre of some of the former boxers in the stands a nod to that.

Champions know champions. Five Welsh world title winners were in the capital to watch their compatriot do something never been done before.

From Cinderella Man Steve Robinson and Barry Jones, to the more recent Joe Cordina, who may still be eyeing a stadium return of his own in the coming weeks.

All have been proud to fly the flag, but perhaps none have worn it quite as much on their sleeve - or shorts - as Price has done.

Here, entering to the strains of a Welsh male voice choir, the atmosphere moved from Friday night in a city centre to full-blooded patriotism.

The anthem stirred so much Kotaskova couldn't help but raise an eyebrow before stepping out of her corner.

From then, she had no time to savour the moment let alone consider become an opportunity the Czech Republic's first world champion.

She felt flurries of punches from the first moments and struggled with the unrelenting pace set by the champion.

Steely-eyed, Price refused to allow a breath and, while Kotaskova continued to try and come onto the front foot, she was met by angry, but calculated attacks.

Kotaskova's problems only increased when she was cut in the fifth round, the hooks from the home fighter providing no let up.

At one point in the seventh, Kotaskova took a shot so fierce she almost turned her back to say no more, but still she came and still Price went hunting with hooks.

She could not find the decisive blow, finally letting the tempo slip, and even enjoying the final seconds as she accepted she had done more than enough to win and win a place in boxing history.

Price was not the only Welsh winner on the night as Rhys Edwards secured a significant victory over Lee McGregor, taking an unanimous decision to claim the WBA Continental featherweight championship.

McGregor, 29, had stepped back down to featherweight after two defeats in his last three bouts and had made it clear he knew his chances of returning to world-challenging level was on the line.

His determination to keep coming forward showed what it meant, soaking up several clean shots, but Edwards proved too quick and too sharp.

The 26-year-old from Penygraig also had something to prove after a disappointing draw with Gully Powar last time out.

Then he faded in the latter round, but here Edwards managed to take McGregor's punches and maintain his own pace. It ensured what is perhaps the biggest win of his career, and to leave McGregor contemplating his options.

Elsewhere on the undercard, Willy Gilheaney's unbeaten record was taken away by the experience of Argentinean Alberto Igancio Palmetta, the former Olympic boxer showing plenty of know-how to overcome the Swansea fighter's guts and early control to take an unanimous points win.

Earlier in the night, Doncaster's Jake Goodwin took the decision in a game middleweight bout with Liverpool fighter Sean Arkwright. Goodwin – who had former world featherweight champion Josh Warrington in his corner – had only accepted the fight on two weeks' notice, accepting before he was even granted time off work.

And there were wins for Welsh fighters Brandon Scott and Kane Shepherd, while Cardigan's Josh Mellor and Newport's Lewis Howells fought to a draw.

SportsTab.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli fastest but penalty means Max Verstappen will start on pole
SportsTab.text:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

SportsTab.title: England v New Zealand: Hosts aim to extend All Black misery
SportsTab.text:
There is a string of symbols tattooed on to Will Stuart's left foot.

A circle, two triangles, an up arrow, another circle, R1, L2, an up arrow, a triangle, and, finally L1 three times.

If you know, in this week of all weeks, you know.

England and British and Irish Lions star Stuart is indelibly, if jokingly, stamped with a Grand Theft Auto cheat code,, external which gives your character maximum in-game sex appeal.

In the absence of the injured Stuart and his cheat code at the start of this year, England certainly lost their mojo.

They had a terrible Six Nations. They were comfortably held at bay by South Africa. Five straight defeats ramped up pressure on the squad and their staff.

Stuart has now returned from a ruptured Achilles tendon and, with him, so has England's swagger.

Against Australia and Japan, England scored 20 tries.

They are ranked top of the Nations Championship for points scored and entries into the opposition 22m. Their attack has shown dexterity of a card sharp, with the sophistication of a socialite.

Those are the sort of intricacies needed to befuddle the best defences.

"We want England to support us. We want to bring joy to them," said head coach Steve Borthwick this week.

So far, this autumn, that objective has been achieved. Twickenham has been seduced by two charismatic displays which have been high on entertainment, if low on jeopardy.

Saturday will undoubtedly be different.

New Zealand are sore. Last weekend's defeat by Wales - their first in 73 years - stung. Coach Dave Rennie's public accusation that the players had "let the country down" will have salted wounds.

He may well have said the same of the insipid performance the team put up in a 33-19 defeat by England last year, under his predecessor Scott Robertson.

The Rennie-ssance overseen by their new boss, with wins over France, Ireland and South Africa in his first few months in charge, has given way to talk of looming crisis.

All Black backs are up hard against a brick wall. And big names - Will Jordan, Jordie Barrett, Cam Roigard and Damian McKenzie - are back to blast their way out of a hole.

England have had their fun over the past couple of weeks.

One of the benefits of being in the northern half of the Nations Championship is a steadier supply of fodder.

Fiji and Japan - the two teams invited to fill out the southern half of the new competition - have won only one of 10 games between them and have a combined points difference of minus 257.

Despite last week's reverse, New Zealand - along with world champions South Africa - are where southern-hemisphere quality is concentrated. And where England's revival will be truly stress-tested.

The comeback of Stuart, and others, has been key for England.

England made a clean sweep of their last autumn campaign, with a high-calibre set of replacements key.

Any lingering final-quarter hopes for the visitors were flushed out by England's depth on the bench.

Stuart is playing the front-row super-sub once again. Fin Baxter - another long-time injury absentee - starts at loosehead, to allow England to rotate between two top-class front rows.

George Martin - an old-school second row enforcer who is recently back from his own 14-month lay-off - is on a bench, also including Henry Pollock and Marcus Smith, loaded with stardust and points to prove.

SportsTab.title: Tom Brady: NFL great could buy Chelsea stake
SportsTab.text:
American football great Tom Brady is looking to invest in Chelsea through ownership group Clearlake Capital.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner has recently divested his stake in Championship club Birmingham City, which he bought into following Tom Wagner's Knighthead Capital takeover in 2023.

It now appears he could move into Chelsea, where he has a positive relationship with influential co-owner Behdad Eghbali, having been a star guest at the after-party following the club's Club World Cup triumph in 2025.

Brady would have no voting rights or control at Chelsea, although the ownership group could look to appoint him to the board if it suited all parties.

The move is not said to be linked to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter's £950m sale of their stakes to Clearlake Capital, which must be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss remains a significant minority stakeholder at Stamford Bridge.

The investment is also not part of a funding round, according to senior sources, and is not intended to dilute Clearlake Capital's control.

However, other interested parties are said to have approached them about investing since Boehly and Walter agreed a deal to leave.

Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Following the end of his playing career he acquired a stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.

On top of that, Brady's commitments include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

SportsTab.title: Grand Slam of Darts: Gerwyn Price survives match darts to reach semi-finals
SportsTab.text:
Gerwyn Price faced two match darts before winning a thrilling quarter-final against Nico Springer at the Grand Slam of Darts, as Luke Littler's conqueror Jermaine Wattimena was knocked out.

Three-time champion Price led for most of the match but his German opponent refused to let him out of reach.

Springer missed a number of chances to level, including three darts at double top to make it 13-13 as he fell 14-12 behind, before he eventually made it 14-14 and then took a 15-14 lead.

However, Price produced a stunning 143 checkout to take it to a decider in which Springer had the throw.

The German left himself 73 after his 16th 180, only to miss double eight and double four for the match prior to Price taking out 78 with treble 18 and double 12.

"I'm quite lucky to come through that game," Price told Sky Sports. "I missed so many chances - I should've punished him.

"I kept him in the game, I kept missing doubles after doubles. Even though he was scoring as well as I was, I was missing opportunities after opportunities but I'm glad I had another one at the end."

SportsTab.title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz beats Flavio Cobolli to continue unbeaten run
SportsTab.text:
A ruthless Carlos Alcaraz put aside his injury concerns to dismantle Flavio Cobolli and ensure a perfect record in the ATP Finals group stages.

Spain's Alcaraz hurt his left hamstring in his previous match against Daniil Medvedev and had a scan on the injury on Thursday.

He arrived for his match against Cobolli with strapping on his upper-left leg - as well as tape on his right knee and a sleeve on his right arm - but was brutally efficient in a 6-4 6-1 win.

The seven-time Grand Slam champion did not face a break point and bludgeoned 29 winners in a 65-minute victory.

"I tried not to move that much. I tried to be aggressive, to dominate the match as much as I can," the 23-year-old said.

"I'm just really happy that I am getting more confident, the way I'm hitting the ball and seeing what's going on in the match.

"The challenge now is not on the court, it's off the court, to do whatever it takes to be in a good shape and feel physically ready for a battle tomorrow."

Alcaraz is now on a 12-match winning streak and will face Ben Shelton, who he beat in the Paris Masters final last month, in Saturday's semi-finals.

Medvedev will take on Alexander Zverev in the other last-four match after beating American Frances Tiafoe in straight sets in their winner-takes-all encounter.

The world number five came through 6-3 6-4 in an hour and 22 minutes.

Alcaraz was conservative in his movement, trying to avoid sliding in and out of the corners - but rather than diminishing his game, it allowed him to produce some astonishing shot-making.

Cobolli never looked as though he had the belief that he could challenge Alcaraz, and was broken in the first game of the match by a thumping return winner.

Alcaraz kept the points short, hammering his forehand and backhand to all corners, and targeted Cobolli's second serve in particular.

An astonishing whipped 110mph forehand winner was the highlight of the first set, which Alcaraz wrapped up with a strong service hold.

Cobolli again lost his serve in the opening game of the second set and Alcaraz claimed five of the final six games to secure victory.

After converting match point with another return winner, Alcaraz embraced Cobolli at the net and offered the crushed Italian a few words of support.

Alcaraz has not had his serve broken once in his three group matches as he bids for a first title at the season-ending event.

He and world number one Zverev have both made it through the group stages without dropping a set, while Alcaraz has not lost more than four games in a set.

In the doubles, Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison reached the semi-finals with a 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 victory over Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos.

The US Open champions will face fourth seeds Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic for a place in Sunday's final.

SportsTab.title: Manchester United fan criticism has gone too far at times - Omar Berrada
SportsTab.text:
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.

Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."

Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.

He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."
SportsTab.description: Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line". In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters...

SportsTab.title: Netball Horizon Series: England men prepare for historic Jamaica ties with potential World Cup on cards.
SportsTab.text:
It's not that men aren't playing it - it's just that you're not seeing it.

That is the message echoed by both James Thomson-Boston - captain of the England men's netball side - and Jamaica defender Authorn Chambers.

These two men's sides have history, and are about to meet again.

In a historic first, their matches will be played as curtain-raisers before England's women, ranked third in the world, face fourth-placed Jamaica in the Vitality Netball Horizon Series in London this weekend.

With an inaugural men's World Cup on the cards, likely within the next few years, BBC Sport looks at the signs that indicate that, if not already, the men's game will soon be on your radar.

The narrative of women's sport fighting for recognition in a historically male-dominated space is a familiar one, but in netball - traditionally a female sport - it is quite the opposite.

Yet in recent years, the rise of the men's game has been meteoric.

The England men's team, known as the Thorns - in contrast to the women's Roses - played their first international in October 2022 and are now coached by women's Netball Super League coach Jo Noel.

They have played international Test series against the likes of Australia, toured St Kitts & Nevis for the Americas Netball Men's Championship, and are now set to play Jamaica for the first time on home soil.

Overseas, Australia and New Zealand contest the Trans-Tasman Cup, while African nations play in the Africa Netball Cup.

And now, 63 years after the first women's World Cup, the sport's global governing body, World Netball, says plans are being developed to host an inaugural men's edition.

In a statement to BBC Sport, it said: "World Netball will always remain proud of the sport's unique female-focused foundations; however we are also a sport that is open to all. We should celebrate and be proud of our traditions but not a hostage to them.

"World Netball feels that now is the right time to intentionally build men into our ecosystem and provide them with an elite platform through which to showcase their skills to the world."

For Chambers, a potential World Cup represents a huge opportunity to get even more eyes on the men's game.

"It needs to be in those kind of spaces that people are seeing it - that's how it's going to grow," he said.

"This sport deserves to have a spotlight on it, be it female or male or altogether," Thomson-Boston added. "I think we just need to keep pushing and keep shouting about it because visibility is key.

"If every men's netball game around the world was now streamed somewhere, you got a notification, you'd realise how many people are actually playing the sport day in, day out."

Thomson-Boston moved to England from Australia 10 years ago. While searching for a netball club to join, he was asked if he actually meant a football club.

Now the questions he is asked are often by mothers of young boys, keen to get their sons involved in netball.

"People always apologise in the DMs - 'I'm so sorry to do this', and I'm like, 'no, flood the DMs. Ask every question you want, because you're going to love it when you step out on court'."

Along with that, Thomson-Boston believes the perception of men playing what is, at its roots, a female-led sport, continues to change - even since the captain last spoke to BBC Sport in May 2025.

Instead of people saying "a guy playing men's netball, that seems a bit strange", he says this has now shifted to excitement and curiosity: "How do you train? How do I find out more about it?"

In England the picture is similar, but at a club level.

Last year, the England Men's & Mixed Netball Association (EMMNA) launched its first men's Super League.

The England Thorns meet once or twice a month to train in Birmingham, but also train with their respective men's clubs - as well as women's Netball Super League (NSL) sides.

"So many people ask me, 'what happens if the men's game gets bigger? Is it going to start dominating this space that has always been a proudly female-led sport?'" said Thomson-Boston.

The answer to the latter question, he says, is a resounding no. Instead, the aim is solely to grow the sport collectively.

"Because the more eyes on the sport, the more people who enjoy the sport, the more people who play it week in, week out, the more people who start attending Super League - the more sponsors can start to look at the sport as a profitable experience for them."

SportsTab.title: Mykhailo Mudryk accuses Andriy Shevchenko of lying about drugs test claims
SportsTab.text:
Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.

Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.

In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".

Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk.

"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong."

Mudryk also said the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.

BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

SportsTab.title: Man Utd drone incident: Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola says filming training sessions by drone should be illegal
SportsTab.text:
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.

"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."

Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.

"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.

"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."

Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.

But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.

"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.

"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.

"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

SportsTab.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
SportsTab.text:
Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.

Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, especially in troublesome times. He will love the pageantry and event glamour of Old Trafford. And he will love having Ferguson in the crowd for the matches.

Pochettino first encountered him in January 2013 when, in his second Southampton game, he went to Old Trafford to face Ferguson’s United, who won 2-1. Pochettino has mentioned that this week. And the meal at Scott’s. And how he was at the Camp Nou for Ferguson’s finest hour: the 1999 Champions League final victory against Bayern Munich. Pochettino was an Espanyol player at the time, together with Toni Jiménez, who is part of his coaching staff, and they watched the first half from so-so seats before blagging their way into the directors’ box for the second period.

When Solskjær scored his iconic late winner, Pochettino and Jiménez celebrated wildly. They were caught up in the moment. It was the first time Pochettino felt a connection to United and he began to pay more attention to them. And Ferguson. Pochettino described him this week as “the best coach in the history of the sport” but it was not a soundbite of convenience. He has always maintained this and said so on the record after the lunch at Scott’s.

How can Pochettino position himself in terms of the Glazers and Ratcliffe? The first thing to say is that he does have experience of unpopular and/or difficult owners. At Spurs, Daniel Levy was forever maligned by the fans, and Pochettino had problems with the American ownership at Chelsea. Between times, the Qataris at PSG were not easy. Pochettino worked to build a relationship with Levy, regularly saying nice things about him in the press and famously including him on a staff-bonding trip to Argentina.

It featured white-water rafting and ended with Pochettino having to fish Levy out of the Manso River. A repeat of the adventure with Joel Glazer feels unlikely but Pochettino’s starting point at United has been to stress unity; the need to create chemistry with everyone, including “the directors and the owners”.

And so to Anfield, where Pochettino first managed with Southampton in September 2013 when his team won 1-0. He has not tasted victory in his eight subsequent trips; seven with Spurs, one with Chelsea, the record shows two draws and six defeats. No United fan expects anything this time but Pochettino considers it a great game to have. He will certainly learn a lot about his players.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
TechnologyTab.text:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

TechnologyTab.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
TechnologyTab.text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".

As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.

"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."

Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.

Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.

"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.

"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

TechnologyTab.title: Thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret operation
TechnologyTab.text:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.
